description: Prefer fd over find, rg over grep -r, cargo nextest over cargo test and dust over du when they are installed (fd may be named fdfind), with a cheat sheet shown once per session.

find-fd.message:
find is blocked in favour of {found}: much faster, and it respects .gitignore. {found} cannot express some find predicates (-perm, -newer REF, -atime/-ctime, -printf beyond paths, -inum, -samefile, -links, -ok, OR across different predicate kinds); for those the original command is fine.

── {found} cheat sheet (`{found} -h` prints the short help) ──
TRAPS — read first:
  {found} skips .gitignore'd paths AND dot-files/dirs by default; find doesn't.
    Want everything?  {found} -u (= -H -I)
  {found} takes a REGEX on the basename: `{found} *.py` is a shell-glob trap → {found} -e py or {found} -g '*.py';  -p matches the full path
  Under sudo, brew binaries are not on secure_path:  sudo "$(command -v {found})" …

{found} [flags] [regex] [path…]   smart-case; -g glob, -F literal, --exact whole name; `{found} -- '-x'` for patterns starting with -
  find . -name '*.py'              →  {found} -e py            (or {found} -g '*.py')
  find . -iname '*foo*'            →  {found} foo              (find . -name foo, exact → {found} --exact foo)
  find . -type f|d|l               →  {found} -t f | -t d | -t l    (-t x executables, -t e empty)
  find . -maxdepth 2 / -mindepth 1 →  {found} -d 2 / --min-depth 1   (--exact-depth N)
  find . -path '*/node_modules' -prune -o …  →  {found} -E node_modules   (glob, repeatable)
  find . -mtime -1 / -mmin -30     →  {found} --changed-within 1d / 30min    (--changed-before 2weeks; mtime only)
  find . -size +10M                →  {found} -S +10mi         (find's M is MiB = mi; m = MB; unit required: b k m g t ki mi gi ti)
  find . -user core                →  {found} --owner core     (--owner :group, '!user' negates)
  find . -exec cmd {{}} \;           →  {found} … -x cmd {{}}     ({{/}} name, {{//}} dir, {{.}} no ext; -x last; PARALLEL, no shell; -j1 = sequential)
  find . -exec cmd {{}} + / -delete  →  {found} … -X cmd / -X rm
  find . -xdev                     →  {found} --one-file-system;   -L follows symlinks;   -0 for xargs -0;   -a absolute paths
  no extension: {found} '^[^.]+$' -t f;   OR by regex: {found} '\.(py|js)$';   {found} PAT --and PAT2;   --format '{{//}}' prints path fields only

Combine with rg: `find … | xargs grep` is usually just `rg PAT [path]`.
  Filters rg lacks (size, mtime, owner, depth, file type) → {found} … -X rg -n PAT   or   {found} -0 … | xargs -0 rg PAT

messages.text:
find … -exec / -delete is blocked in favour of {found}, which runs the command itself:
{found} [regex | -g GLOB] [path…] then
  -x cmd {{}}   per file, like -exec cmd {{}} \;   ({{/}} name, {{//}} dir, {{.}} no extension; -x goes last)
  -X cmd       all files in one call, like -exec cmd {{}} +
  -X rm        like -delete
TRAPS: -x runs in PARALLEL and with no shell: add -j1 for find's one-at-a-time order, and wrap pipes or redirects in sh -c '…' {{}}.
  {found} skips .gitignore'd and hidden paths by default (-u includes them); the pattern is a REGEX on the basename (-e py, -g '*.py').
{found} cannot express -perm, -newer REF, -atime/-ctime, -printf beyond paths, -inum, -samefile, -links, -ok or OR across predicate kinds; for those the original command is fine. `{found} -h` prints the short help.

find-fd.messageShort:
find is blocked in favour of {found}: much faster, and it respects .gitignore. {found} cannot express some find predicates (-perm, -newer REF, -atime/-ctime, -printf beyond paths, -inum, -samefile, -links, -ok, OR across different predicate kinds); for those the original command is fine.

{found} [regex | -g GLOB] [path]   (-e ext, -t f|d, -d depth, -E exclude, -u = ignored+hidden, -x/-X cmd = -exec)
   pattern is a REGEX on the basename — `{found} *.py` is a shell trap, use -e py; -p to match the path
(The full cheat sheet was shown earlier in this session; `{found} -h` prints the short help.)

grep-rg.description: recursive grep when ripgrep is installed
grep-rg.message:
grep -r is blocked in favour of rg: much faster, and it respects .gitignore.

── rg cheat sheet (`rg -h` prints the short help) ──
TRAPS — read first:
  rg skips .gitignore'd paths AND dot-files/dirs by default; grep -r doesn't.
    Want everything?  rg -uu (= --no-ignore --hidden; -uuu adds --binary, but only -a prints binary matches)
  rg's first non-flag arg is the PATTERN: `rg src/` searches for the text "src/" (exit 0, no warning) → rg PAT src/
  rg silently skips binary files (grep prints "Binary file matches"); -a searches them as text
  Under sudo, brew binaries are not on secure_path:  sudo "$(command -v rg)" …

rg [flags] PATTERN [path…]       case-sensitive by default; line numbers + per-file headings automatic; -w -x -F -v -o -A -B -C as in grep
  grep -rn foo .                   →  rg foo              (-N no line numbers, -H/-I force/suppress filenames)
  grep -ri foo                     →  rg -i foo           (-S smart-case, -s force sensitive)
  grep -r --include='*.py' foo     →  rg -t py foo   or   rg -g '*.py' foo      (rg --type-list; -g beats -t)
  grep -r --exclude-dir=vendor     →  rg -g '!vendor' foo       (include-globs for dirs need /**: -g 'src/**'; later globs win; -T py = not type)
  grep -rl / -rL / -rc             →  rg -l / --files-without-match / -c    (-c omits 0-count files: --include-zero; --count-matches = per match)
  grep -rE … / -rP …               →  rg …  / rg -P …     (-P for look-around and backreferences);  `rg -e -foo` for patterns starting with -
  grep -ro foo                     →  rg -o foo           (-r REPL rewrites output only, never files)
  grep -rz … / multi-line          →  rg -z … (decompressor must be on PATH; silent if missing) / rg -U 'a\nb' (`.` needs --multiline-dotall to cross lines)
  find . -type f | …               →  rg --files [path]   (candidate files under the same ignore rules; a real search additionally skips binaries)
  -m N max per file, --max-filesize 5M, --sort path for stable order

Combine: rg walks the tree itself, so `find … | xargs grep` is usually just `rg PAT [path]`.
  Filters rg lacks (size, mtime, owner, depth, file type) → list the files with fd (fdfind on Debian and Ubuntu): fd … -X rg -n PAT   or   fd -0 … | xargs -0 rg PAT
grep-rg.messageShort:
grep -r is blocked in favour of rg: much faster, and it respects .gitignore.

rg PATTERN [path]              (-t py / -g '*.py', -l, -i, -w, -F, -C3, -uu = ignored+hidden)
   first arg is the PATTERN — `rg src/` searches for the text "src/"; pass the dir as the 2nd arg
(The full cheat sheet was shown earlier in this session; `rg -h` prints the short help.)

cargo-nextest.description: cargo test when cargo-nextest is installed (doctests exempt)
cargo-nextest.message:
cargo test is blocked in favour of cargo nextest run (installed): every test runs in its own process, so one failing or hanging test cannot disturb the others, and the run is faster. The usual flags carry over: `--workspace`, `-p NAME`, `--no-run`, a test-name filter (`cargo nextest run my_test`), `--no-capture` to see test output.
Doctests are the exception: nextest cannot run them, so `cargo test --doc` is the one case that needs plain cargo test (it is not blocked); run it separately when the crate has doctests.

messages.text:
cargo test … --nocapture is blocked in favour of cargo nextest run (installed): drop the `--` and the libtest flag, write `--no-capture`, and keep the rest as it is (`--workspace`, `-p NAME`, a test-name filter): `cargo test -p foo my_test -- --nocapture` becomes `cargo nextest run -p foo my_test --no-capture`. --no-capture also runs the tests one at a time.
Doctests need plain `cargo test --doc` (not blocked).
messages.messageShort: cargo test is blocked in favour of cargo nextest run; `-- --nocapture` is `--no-capture` (`cargo nextest run -p foo my_test --no-capture`). Only `cargo test --doc` needs plain cargo test.

cargo-nextest.messageShort: cargo test is blocked in favour of cargo nextest run (same flags: `--workspace`, `-p NAME`, a test-name filter, `--no-capture`); only `cargo test --doc` needs plain cargo test.

du-dust.message:
du is blocked in favour of dust (installed): it sorts by size and draws a bar chart, so no `| sort -h | head` is needed.
  dust -d 1 PATH   the biggest entries one level down (the biggest is last; -r puts it first)
  dust -n 20 PATH  only the 20 biggest lines
  dust -d 0 PATH   just the total, one line, like du -sh PATH
  dust -s PATH     apparent size (file length) instead of disk blocks
  -b hides the percent bars and -c the colours (use both when you read or pipe the output); -o k|m|g|si sets the unit.
dust cannot replace du where another program parses the output (byte-exact `du -sk` / `-sb`, `du --max-depth` in a pipeline): if you really need du, repeat the same command and it will run.

messages.text:
du -s is blocked in favour of `dust -d 0 PATH` (installed): it prints the same one total line; add `-s` for apparent size and `-o k|m|g|si` for the unit. For a breakdown use `dust -d 1 PATH` (biggest entries one level down, the biggest last; -r puts it first, -n 20 limits the lines).
dust cannot replace du where another program parses the output (byte-exact `du -sk` / `-sb`, `du --max-depth` in a pipeline): if you really need du, repeat the same command and it will run.
messages.messageShort: du -s is blocked in favour of `dust -d 0 PATH` (one total line; `-s` apparent size); `dust -d 1 PATH` for a breakdown. If you really need du (byte-exact `du -sk`, parsed output), repeat the same command.

messages.text:
du with a depth limit is blocked in favour of `dust -d N PATH` (installed): the same depth, the entries sorted by size (the biggest last; -r puts it first), `-n 20` limits the lines, `-s` is apparent size, `-b -c` drop the bars and colours.
dust cannot replace du where another program parses the output (byte-exact `du -sk` / `-sb`, `du --max-depth` in a pipeline): if you really need du, repeat the same command and it will run.
messages.messageShort: du -d is blocked in favour of `dust -d N PATH` (sorted by size; `-n 20` limits the lines). If you really need du (parsed output), repeat the same command.

du-dust.messageShort: du is blocked in favour of dust: `dust -d 1 PATH` (biggest entries one level down), `dust -d 0 PATH` (total only), `-n 20` limits lines, `-s` apparent size, `-b -c` no bars or colours. If you really need du (byte-exact `du -sk`, parsed output), repeat the same command.
